title: Tandem
summary: Peer-to-peer sync between the devices of one collection, over the local network.
description: A collection is the data a set of devices share; each product that uses this part says what its collection is. The devices sync directly with each other on the local network, without a server.
groundwork: The collection is kept in one SQLite database per device.

groundwork.text: Every table that syncs has a primary key that two devices can't both make, so rows made on different devices never collide by key.
ways: random ids (UUIDv4, or UUIDv7 to keep them in time order) made by the app
existing integer keys migrated to random ids, with the references to them

groundwork.text: The app's SQLite can load an extension at startup, on every platform the app runs on.
ways: SQLite opened from native code that the app controls, with extension loading enabled
a SQLite library that bundles the extension

groundwork.text: The app's database schema changes only through migrations, which run in order on every device, and a part can run its own step after each.
ways: a hook in the migration runner the app already has
migrations moved into a runner that calls back after each one

groundwork: The app runs as a native app on each of its platforms, so it can listen and send on the local network.
The app has settings the user can open, and a part can add a section of its own to them.

stories.as: someone who uses the app on more than one device
stories.want: the same data on each of them
stories.soThat: I can pick up wherever I left off

requirements.text: Two instances of the app on the same local network can sync their databases with each other.
No data of the collection passes through a server during sync.
Every table syncs unless it is explicitly local to the device.
Settings that belong to one device (sync bookmarks, caches) are never synced.
A database restored from an older copy is detected at startup, or at its first sync if its marker was restored with it, and then takes a new device id and syncs from scratch.
On Android, sync also runs while the app is closed.
Development and release builds never sync with each other.
On macOS the app is code-signed, ad hoc at the least, so macOS asks before letting it onto the local network instead of keeping it off without asking.
